scenes.tts: Red and green image channels overlap. Does the yellow patch mean the two proteins bind? Chapter one showed why close objects merge into one spot. Now follow the evidence from label to claim.
scenes.visual: Open on chapter 1's optical bench, same layout and colours: dark cell at left, blue objective in the centre, detector screen at right. In the cell, replace the two green vesicles with a green-labelled mitochondrion outline (cartoon tube) and scattered red dots for a second label. On the detector, green and red images slide over each other and the shared region blends to bright yellow-orange. A large question 'Do they bind?' rises above the yellow patch as the question is spoken. Mark the cell picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Red and green image channels overlap. Does the yellow patch mean the two proteins bind? Chapter one showed why close objects merge into one spot. Now follow the evidence from label to claim.

scenes.visual: Keep the bench and the slowly pulsing yellow patch. Dim slightly and show the title 'What an Overlap Can Claim' across the upper third for two seconds, then clear it without moving the bench.

scenes.tts: Start with the blur from chapter one. Across the image, it is about two hundred thirty nanometres wide. Along the depth direction, it stretches to about eight hundred nanometres. A yellow pixel alone cannot show that the two sources are closer than this scale.
scenes.caption: Start with the blur from chapter one. Across the image, it is about 230 nanometres wide. Along the depth direction, it stretches to about 800 nanometres. A yellow pixel alone cannot show that the two sources are closer than this scale.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one yellow pixel on the detector. From it, grow the chapter 1 Airy blur, then extrude it into a soft 3D ellipsoid (an elongated grain of rice standing upright along the optical axis). A yellow bracket across its width reads 'about 230 nm'; a taller yellow bracket along its height reads 'about 800 nm' with a small arrow labelled 'depth'. Label the soft-edged ellipsoid 'resolution scale' and mark it 'schematic, not a boundary'. Green and red dots drift slowly inside it.
scenes.narration: Start with the blur from chapter one. Across the image, it is about 230 nanometres wide. Along the depth direction, it stretches to about 800 nanometres. A yellow pixel alone cannot show that the two sources are closer than this scale.

scenes.tts: These dimensions use chapter one's green-light settings. A red channel usually has a longer emission wavelength and a larger blur. For a two-colour claim, use the measured resolution of each channel.
scenes.visual: Keep the soft green ellipsoid and its two brackets. Add a red ellipsoid in the same position and let it expand slightly beyond the green one as 'longer wavelength' appears. Replace both with one badge reading 'measure each channel'. Mark both ellipsoids 'schematic'; do not imply a universal red-channel size.
scenes.narration: These dimensions use chapter one's green-light settings. A red channel usually has a longer emission wavelength and a larger blur. For a two-colour claim, use the measured resolution of each channel.

scenes.tts: Here is a question to hold. At typical cellular protein density, how many protein molecules would this volume contain? A handful, a few hundred, or tens of thousands?
scenes.visual: Keep the ellipsoid centred and filling most of the frame height. Beside it, stack three option cards that slide in one by one as they are spoken: 'a handful', 'a few hundred', 'tens of thousands'. Above, the question card 'HOW MANY INSIDE?' in large white text. The green and red dots keep drifting inside the ellipsoid; do not reveal the answer.
scenes.narration: Here is a question to hold. At typical cellular protein density, how many protein molecules would this volume contain? A handful, a few hundred, or tens of thousands?

scenes.visual: Hold the full prediction frame for 4.5 seconds: ellipsoid, three option cards and 'HOW MANY FIT?' unchanged. Only the drifting dots move.

scenes.tts: Treat the blur as an ellipsoid. Its volume is roughly two hundredths of a cubic micrometre. At typical cellular protein density, it contains tens of thousands of protein molecules.
scenes.caption: Treat the blur as an ellipsoid. Its volume is roughly 0.02 cubic micrometres. At typical cellular protein density, it contains tens of thousands of protein molecules.
scenes.visual: Highlight the 'tens of thousands' card and dim the other two. Replace the cards with one large badge reading 'about 0.02 cubic micrometres' and a second badge reading 'tens of thousands, cellular density'. Keep the soft ellipsoid behind them, marked 'order-of-magnitude estimate' and 'schematic'. Use a density glow rather than drawing thousands of separate particles.
scenes.narration: Treat the blur as an ellipsoid. Its volume is roughly 0.02 cubic micrometres. At typical cellular protein density, it contains tens of thousands of protein molecules.

scenes.tts: So, after the controls, an in-focus overlap can support proximity within about this volume. It does not say the two proteins touch. In widefield, out-of-focus haze can create apparent overlap from farther away.
scenes.visual: Keep the soft ellipsoid with one red and one green dot far apart inside it, under a badge labelled 'in-focus'. Draw a white line between them labelled 'not touching'. Then replace the badge with 'widefield haze' as faint green signal drifts in from above and below the ellipsoid and adds to the yellow pixel. Mark the whole picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: So, after the controls, an in-focus overlap can support proximity within about this volume. It does not say the two proteins touch. In widefield, out-of-focus haze can create apparent overlap from farther away.

scenes.tts: Even that weaker claim needs evidence. Colour overlap is a claim about proximity. It is only as strong as each link that produced it. Check three links in turn.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full bench. Along the light path from cell to detector, three large chain links appear in sequence and stay: 'label' at the cell, 'channels' at a two-colour filter block after the objective, 'record' at the detector. A fourth link, 'claim', hangs off the detector's yellow patch. A soft pulse travels along the chain from cell to claim.
scenes.narration: Even that weaker claim needs evidence. Colour overlap is a claim about proximity. It is only as strong as each link that produced it. Check three links in turn.

scenes.tts: First, the label. An antibody can bind the wrong protein. Signal loss after knockout supports specificity. With knockdown, the signal should fall with verified target reduction. A secondary-only sample checks nonspecific signal from the fluorescent secondary.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto the 'label' link at the cell. Show a rounded blob labelled 'primary' binding a block labelled 'target', then a second rounded blob with a green glow labelled 'secondary' binding the primary. Transform that diagram into two side-by-side cartoon cells marked 'schematic': one labelled 'target knockout', one labelled 'secondary only'. Leave both images blank grey with question marks; do not show what either looks like. Never draw a molecular structure; antibodies are simple labelled blobs.
scenes.narration: First, the label. An antibody can bind the wrong protein. Signal loss after knockout supports specificity. With knockdown, the signal should fall with verified target reduction. A secondary-only sample checks nonspecific signal from the fluorescent secondary.

scenes.tts: Second, the channels. A dye's light can leak into another colour channel. That leak is called bleed-through. Single-label samples measure it, and multicolour beads test whether the channels line up. Misregistration can separate matching signals or superimpose different ones.
scenes.visual: Move to the 'channels' link: a filter block splits light into a green channel panel and a red channel panel. A thin green stream reaches the red panel; label it 'bleed-through'. Transform the stream into a single-label sample whose red panel shows a faint ghost labelled 'measured leak'. Replace that sample with a few schematic beads visible in both panels; first offset the panels, then slide the red panel into alignment and label it 'registered'.
scenes.narration: Second, the channels. A dye's light can leak into another colour channel. That leak is called bleed-through. Single-label samples measure it, and multicolour beads test whether the channels line up. Misregistration can separate matching signals or superimpose different ones.

scenes.tts: Third, the record. Image every condition with identical settings. Keep the relevant pixels below the detector maximum. Background subtraction removes the average background, but not its photon noise.
scenes.visual: Move to the 'record' link at the detector. Show two detector panels labelled 'control' and 'treated' with one shared settings dial between them, both needles at the same position, labelled 'identical settings'. Replace them with a vertical pixel-value gauge whose top red line reads 'detector maximum'; a bright level rises and stops below the line. Replace the gauge with a computed noisy intensity trace. When 'subtract background' is applied, its mean drops while its wiggle remains; label the wiggle 'photon noise remains'.
scenes.narration: Third, the record. Image every condition with identical settings. Keep the relevant pixels below the detector maximum. Background subtraction removes the average background, but not its photon noise.

scenes.tts: Now return to yellow. If every link holds, an in-focus overlap supports proximity at roughly one resolution volume. Binding is a separate claim, and it needs other experiments. Co-immunoprecipitation supports membership in the same complex, but not direct contact. A test with purified proteins addresses direct interaction.
scenes.visual: Back to the full bench with all three chain links glowing. The yellow patch on the detector connects to the ellipsoid from scene 3, labelled 'proximity at resolution scale'. A separate box to the right labelled 'binding' stays outlined, not filled. Two dashed arrows lead toward it: one from a cartoon bead with two blocks attached, labelled 'co-IP: same complex', and one from a small cartoon test tube labelled 'purified proteins: direct binding'. Mark the box and test tube 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Now return to yellow. If every link holds, an in-focus overlap supports proximity at roughly one resolution volume. Binding is a separate claim, and it needs other experiments. Co-immunoprecipitation supports membership in the same complex, but not direct contact. A test with purified proteins addresses direct interaction.

scenes.tts: So read a colour overlap the way chapter one read the blur. Ask what was labelled, what leaked between channels, and what the detector recorded. The overlap reports what the measurement could separate, and nothing finer. Overlap supports proximity, not binding.
scenes.visual: Restore the clean two-colour bench with the yellow patch and the faint ellipsoid behind it. Fade the bench while the end-card line appears large and centred: 'Colour overlap shows proximity within one resolution volume, not binding.' Keep a slow green and red shimmer behind the text until the scene ends.
scenes.narration: So read a colour overlap the way chapter one read the blur. Ask what was labelled, what leaked between channels, and what the detector recorded. The overlap reports what the measurement could separate, and nothing finer. Overlap supports proximity, not binding.
